1.title: Hypothesis Forms and Decision Errors
elements: para
Recall hypothesis definition. A hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter that we aim to test using sample data
para

Null and alternate forms. The null hypothesis (H₀) will always be expressed in one of the standard forms and never contains an equality sign; the alternate hypothesis (H₁) also follows a standard form and likewise has no equality sign
para

Judgment outcomes. When evaluating a hypothesis, our judgment can be correct if the ground truth matches the sample evidence, leading to a correct decision to accept or reject H₀; otherwise the judgment is incorrect
para
Type I and Type II errors. A Type I error occurs when we reject H₀ while it is actually true; a Type II error occurs when we fail to reject H₀ while it is actually false
para
Definition of level of significance. The level of significance is the maximum probability of making a Type I error that the researcher is willing to accept
para

Alpha and confidence. An alpha value of 0.05 corresponds to a 95 % confidence level, while an alpha of 0.01 corresponds to a 99 % confidence level. The confidence level reflects the small tail probability that we are willing to risk when making a decision

question.q: What is a Type I error in hypothesis testing?
question.answer: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true.

2.title: Test Types, Sampling Distribution, and Rejection Rule
elements: para

Available test distributions. Hypothesis tests may be based on normal, t, F, or chi‑square distributions, but for this course we restrict ourselves to the normal distribution (and the related "feed" distribution)
para

Sampling distribution of the test statistic. Under the null hypothesis we assume a sampling distribution for the chosen statistic; for a normal population this distribution is normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n
para

Two‑tailed versus single‑tailed. A test can be two‑tailed or single‑tailed depending on the alternative hypothesis; in a two‑tailed test the null is rejected if the statistic is either too large or too small relative to critical values on the standard normal curve
para

Rejecting the null hypothesis. We reject the null hypothesis when the observed test statistic falls beyond the upper or lower critical thresholds on the standard normal curve, i.e., when it is too large or too small

question.q: In a two‑tailed test, when is the null hypothesis rejected?
question.answer: When the test statistic is either larger than the upper critical value or smaller than the lower critical value on the standard normal curve

3.title: Z‑Test Derivation and Critical Regions
elements: para

Z‑test statistic. The Z‑score is the sample statistic minus the population mean divided by the population standard deviation. Because the sampling distribution of the sample mean has mean equal to the population mean, the Z‑score follows a standard normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1
para

Critical regions. For a two‑tailed test at significance level 0.05, the critical values are ±1.96. Values of the test statistic falling beyond these limits lie in the rejection region and lead to rejection of the null hypothesis

question.q: What are the critical values for a two‑tailed test at α = 0.05?

4.title: Designing a Decision Rule for a Coin Toss Example
elements: para

Decision rule setup. To design a decision rule, first draw the standard normal curve and mark the critical regions based on the chosen level of significance. The rule states that if the computed Z value lies outside the interval [−z_c, z_c], the null hypothesis is rejected
example

Example (Coin Toss Test): In a sample of 64 tosses of a fair coin, the expected number of heads is μ = 64×0.5 = 32. The decision rule at α = 0.05 is to reject H₀ if the observed number of heads is less than 32−1.96√(64×0.5×0.5) or greater than 32+1.96√(64×0.5×0.5). Steps: Compute μ = 32; Compute σ = √(64×0.5×0.5); Compute critical values 32±1.96σ.

question.q: What is the decision rule for rejecting H₀ in the coin toss example at α = 0.05?
question.answer: Reject H₀ if the number of heads is less than 32−1.96σ or greater than 32+1.96σ

1.title: Course Goals and Success Strategy
elements: para

Course Goals. The course has three main goals: understanding concepts, developing programming skills, and learning problem‑solving through problem sets. Practice is the underlying requirement for all three
para
Success Strategy. Fear of breaking the computer is unfounded because running Anaconda and typing commands cannot damage the system
para

Course Structure. The class is divided into three main sections: learning how to program, understanding control flow, and writing good code. The first section covers how to represent knowledge with data structures and deciding what objects to create
para
Learning how to program involves figuring out what objects to create and how to represent knowledge with data structures.
para
Control Flow. The second part focuses on control flow, where programs make decisions and jump between statements
para
Code Quality. The third part deals with writing good code: readable, modular, and organized so that others can understand it

question.q: What is the underlying requirement for all three main goals of the course?

2.title: Computers and Calculations
elements: para

Computers and Calculations. A computer performs massive numbers of calculations and stores the results in memory. Modern machines can execute on the order of a billion operations per second and have hundreds of gigabytes of storage available. Computers perform two kinds of calculations: low‑level operations built into the language such as addition, subtraction, and multiplication, and higher‑level operations composed from these primitives. A programmer can combine primitive types to define new calculations that the computer will execute as well

question.q: What are the two kinds of calculations a computer performs?
question.answer: Low‑level operations built into the language and higher‑level operations composed from these primitives.

3.title: Declarative vs Imperative Knowledge and Random Selection
elements: para
Declarative knowledge consists of statements of fact that a computer can store. In the lecture, the statement of fact was that someone would win a Google Cardboard before class ends.
para

Imperative knowledge is the recipe or sequence of steps a machine must follow to achieve a goal. The machine must be told how to make someone win a Google Cardboard before class ends, not just that it will happen.
example

Example (Random Selection): The chosen number, 75, was then used to locate the corresponding responder on the sheet. Steps: Import random package; Call random.randint(16,272); Use result to find responder.

question.q: What is the difference between declarative and imperative knowledge?
question.answer: Declarative knowledge is a statement of fact; imperative knowledge is a sequence of steps to achieve a goal.

4.title: Imperative Recipe for Computing Square Roots
elements: para

Imperative recipe. The imperative recipe for finding a square root starts with a guess G, then repeatedly computes G·G and compares it to the target x. If G·G is not close enough, a new guess is formed by averaging G and x/G
para

Control flow. The recipe contains four essential parts: a simple sequence of steps, control decisions about closeness, repeated execution of the steps, and a stopping condition. These parts together form the flow of control for the algorithm
para
Stopping condition. The stopping condition prevents endless execution; it is satisfied when the guess is close enough to the true square root, for example within 0.01 or 0.001 of the target

question.q: What are the four essential parts of an imperative recipe?
question.answer: A simple sequence of steps, control decisions about closeness, repeated execution, and a stopping condition.

5.title: Stored‑Program Computers and Basic Architecture
elements: para

Stored‑program computers can hold a sequence of instructions that the CPU executes, allowing the same hardware to perform different tasks by changing the instruction sequence. This contrasts with fixed‑program computers that could only perform one task.
para

Basic architecture. The basic computer architecture consists of four main parts: memory, input/output, the arithmetic‑logic unit (ALU), and the control unit. Memory stores both data and the instruction sequence; the ALU performs primitive operations such as addition and subtraction; the control unit orchestrates instruction execution; peripherals handle input and output

question.q: What are the four main components of basic computer architecture?
question.answer: Memory, input/output, the arithmetic‑logic unit (ALU), and the control unit.

6.title: Control Flow in Stored‑Program Computers
elements: para

Control Unit and Program Counter. The control unit contains a program counter that holds the address of the next instruction to execute. When a sequence of instructions is loaded, the program counter starts at the first instruction and supplies that instruction to the ALU. After the ALU completes its operation, the program counter increments by one to point to the next instruction in the sequence
para

Branching and Tests. A test instruction compares two values and returns a Boolean result. Depending on whether the result is true or false, the program counter may either advance to the next instruction or jump to a different address, such as the beginning of the program. Thus control flow can skip or repeat instructions
para

Instruction Set Primitives. The primitive operations a stored‑program computer can perform are addition, subtraction, logic operations, tests (equal, less than, etc.), and data movement such as loading and storing. The interpreter decides whether to proceed to the next instruction, skip, or repeat based on these operations

question.q: What determines whether the program counter jumps to a different address during execution?
question.answer: The result of a test instruction (true or false).

7.title: Primitive Operations and Turing Completeness
elements: para
Turing’s Six Primitives. Alan Turing showed that any computation can be achieved with just six primitives: move left, move right, read right, scan, and do nothing
example

Example (Turing’s Six Primitives in Action): A Turing machine can move its head left or right, read the symbol under the head, scan the tape, or do nothing, and by sequencing these actions it can perform any computation. Steps: move left; move right; read right; scan; do nothing.
para

Programming Language Primitives. Programming languages provide a convenient set of primitives so programmers do not have to program only with the six Turing commands. Once a language has a set of primitives, expressions can be built by combining them, and these expressions evaluate to a value with meaning in the language
para

Syntax and Static Semantics. After forming syntactically valid expressions, the next concern is static semantics, which determines whether the meaning is coherent. For example, in English a syntactically valid phrase follows noun‑verb‑noun, while in Python a syntactically valid expression might be an operator followed by another operator
para

Static semantics vs meaning. An expression can be syntactically correct and satisfy static semantics even though it lacks a clear meaning, such as adding a word to a number. In programming languages static semantics checks that operators have appropriate operand types, but it does not guarantee that the operation makes sense in the real world. This mirrors natural language, where a phrase can be grammatically correct yet ambiguous or meaningless, for example the phrase “flying planes can be dangerous” has multiple interpretations

question.q: How many primitives did Turing identify as sufficient for any computation?
